title: 2 Chronicles 8:12–18
context: 2 Chronicles 8:12–18 describes Solomon’s ordering of worship and his trade by sea. He offers burnt offerings according to the commandment of Moses for Sabbaths, new moons, and the three annual feasts, and he appoints priests, Levites, and gatekeepers according to David’s arrangements. The work on the LORD’s house is completed. Solomon goes to Ezion Geber and Eloth, and Huram sends ships and experienced sailors who bring gold from Ophir. The parallel in 1 Kings 9:25–28 says more briefly that Solomon offered three times a year, and it gives four hundred twenty talents of gold where Chronicles gives four hundred fifty. Chronicles also says Huram sent ships, while Kings says Solomon built a fleet with Hiram’s sailors. A talent weighed about 66 pounds. These notes name the differences without harmonizing them. Both traditions read the passage as showing worship carried out according to God’s word and prosperity under God’s blessing.

verses.text: Then Solomon offered burnt offerings to the LORD on the LORD’s altar which he had built before the porch,
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon offers burnt offerings on the LORD’s altar before the porch. Arminians see the king leading the nation in regular worship at the temple, which shows his commitment to God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the offerings as worship according to God’s appointed way. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 9:25 and read the verse as shared ground about faithful worship.

verses.text: even as the duty of every day required, offering according to the commandment of Moses on the Sabbaths, on the new moons, and on the set feasts, three times per year, during the feast of unleavened bread, during the feast of weeks, and during the feast of booths.
verses.arminianNotes: He offers according to the commandment of Moses for Sabbaths, new moons, and the three annual feasts: unleavened bread, weeks, and booths. Arminian readers see worship carried out according to God’s word, with every season of the year marked by offerings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress the Chronicler’s concern that worship follow what God commanded. Both traditions note that 1 Kings 9:25 speaks more briefly of offerings three times a year.

verses.text: He appointed, according to the ordinance of David his father, the divisions of the priests to their service, and the Levites to their offices, to praise and to minister before the priests, as the duty of every day required, the doorkeepers also by their divisions at every gate, for David the man of God had so commanded.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon appoints priests, Levites, and gatekeepers according to David’s ordinance, for David the man of God had commanded it. Arminians see continuity between David’s planning and Solomon’s practice, showing faithful leadership across generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the order of worship as given through David (1 Chronicles 23–26). Both traditions read the verse as showing the Chronicler’s concern for ordered, faithful service at the temple.

verses.text: They didn’t depart from the commandment of the king to the priests and Levites concerning any matter or concerning the treasures.
verses.arminianNotes: They do not depart from the king’s commandment to the priests and Levites in any matter, including the treasures. Arminian readers see faithful obedience among those who served at the temple, a sign of a healthy time in Israel’s worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as an example of God’s blessing on faithful service. Both traditions treat the verse as shared ground and read it as part of the Chronicler’s positive picture of Solomon’s reign.

verses.text: Now all the work of Solomon was accomplished from the day of the foundation of the LORD’s house until it was finished. So the LORD’s house was completed.
verses.arminianNotes: All Solomon’s work is accomplished from the foundation of the LORD’s house until it is finished, so the house is completed. Arminians see the completion as the fruit of faithful work and God’s help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the finished temple as God’s purpose fulfilled through Solomon. Both traditions read the verse as a summary statement that closes the account of the temple building.

verses.text: Then Solomon went to Ezion Geber and to Eloth, on the seashore in the land of Edom.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon goes to Ezion Geber and Eloth on the seashore in Edom. Arminian readers see Solomon extending trade to the Red Sea, and they note the parallel with 1 Kings 9:26.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as part of the record of Solomon’s prosperity. Both traditions hold the exact locations with some caution and avoid building on uncertain identifications.

verses.text: Huram sent him ships and servants who had knowledge of the sea by the hands of his servants; and they came with the servants of Solomon to Ophir, and brought from there four hundred fifty talents of gold, and brought them to King Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes: Huram sends ships and sailors, who go with Solomon’s servants to Ophir and bring four hundred fifty talents of gold. A talent weighed about 66 pounds. Arminians note that 1 Kings 9:28 gives four hundred twenty talents.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and name the difference without harmonizing it. Both traditions note that the location of Ophir is uncertain, and they read the verse as a description of the wealth God gave Solomon.
